'''Richard Alfred Tapia''' (March 25, 1938 – May 22, 2026) was an American mathematician and academic.  He held the title of University Professor at [[Rice University]] in [[Houston]], Texas, the university's highest academic rank.<ref name=NSF2007>{{cite web|access-date=2009-06-06|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward.do?AwardNumber=0634516|title=Award #0634516 &mdash; Empowering Leadership: Computing Scholars of Tomorrow|date= March 1, 2007|publisher=[[National Science Foundation]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081019033656/https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward.do?AwardNumber=0634516|archive-date=October 19, 2008}} Tapia was the [[principal investigator]] on a $2 million NSF grant (2007-2010) addressing networking for a "minority student or faculty at a majority institution".</ref><ref name=UniversityProfessor>{{cite press release|url=http://www.media.rice.edu/media/NewsBot.asp?MODE=VIEW&ID=7839&SnID=197900909|title=Tapia promoted to University Professor: Hispanic pioneer earns university's top academic title|publisher=Rice University|date=October 14, 2005|access-date=November 19, 2005|archive-date=February 6, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120206211457/http://www.media.rice.edu/media/NewsBot.asp?MODE=VIEW&ID=7839&SnID=197900909|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1996 [[Bill Clinton|President Bill Clinton]] awarded Tapia the Presidential Award for Mathematics, Science, and Engineering Mentoring.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ketterer |first=Samantha |date=April 7, 2024 |title=Legendary Rice professor Richard Tapia honored for 50 years of research and mentorship |url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/education/article/rice-tapia-50-years-honor-19381467.php |access-date=April 1, 2025 |website=Houston Chronicle}}</ref> In 2011 [[Barack Obama|President Barack Obama]] awarded Tapia the [[National Medal of Science]].<ref name=NationalMedalofScience>{{cite web|access-date = September 28, 2011|url = http://news.sciencemag.org/scienceinsider/2011/09/twelve-researchers-take-home-top.html?ref=hp
|title = Twelve Researchers Take Home Top MedalsScienceInsider - breaking news and analysis from the world of science policy
|first = David|last = Malakoff|work = Science Insider|date = September 27, 2011|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20111001050151/http://news.sciencemag.org/scienceinsider/2011/09/twelve-researchers-take-home-top.html?ref=hp|archive-date = October 1, 2011}}</ref> He was the Maxfield and Oshman professor of engineering; associate director of graduate studies, Office of Research and Graduate Studies; and director of the Center for Excellence and Equity in Education at Rice University.<ref name=CAAMrat_briefbio>{{cite web|url=http://www.caam.rice.edu/~rat/brief_bio.html|title=Richard A. Tapia &mdash; Brief Bio |publisher=Department of Computational and Applied Mathematics, Rice University}}</ref>

Tapia's mathematical research was centered on [[optimization (mathematics)|mathematical optimization]] and [[iterative method]]s for [[Nonlinearity|nonlinear]] problems, with his most recent work focused on [[algorithms]] for [[constrained optimization]] and [[interior point method]]s for [[linear programming|linear]] and [[nonlinear programming]].

== Early life and education ==
Richard Alfred Tapia was born on March 25, 1938,<ref>{{cite web|title=Richard Alfred Tapia|url=https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/houston-tx/richard-tapia-12898426|publisher=Geo. H. Lewis & Sons Funeral Directors|access-date=June 17, 2026}}</ref><ref name="nyt" /> in [[Santa Monica, California]], to Amado and Magda Tapia, who both immigrated to the United States from Mexico.<ref name=MathTutor-Bio>{{cite web |title=Richard Tapia - Biography |work=Math Tutor Index|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Tapia/ |publisher=St. Andrew's University|access-date=5 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="RiceObit">{{cite news|accessdate=May 23, 2026 |url= https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/richard-tapia-pioneering-mathematician-and-advocate-diversity-passes-away-88
|date=May 23, 2026
|title= Richard Tapia, pioneering mathematician and advocate for diversity, passes away at 88
|first=Rachael
|last=Leeson
|work=Rice News
|publisher=[[Rice University]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260524050022/https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/richard-tapia-pioneering-mathematician-and-advocate-diversity-passes-away-88|archive-date=May 24, 2026}}</ref> He and his twin brother were the oldest of five siblings, with two younger brothers and sister.<ref name=MathTutor-Bio/> His father worked for Japanese-American [[horticulture|horticulturist]]s in southern California.<ref>{{cite book |title=Hispanic Engineer & IT |date=2010 |publisher=Career Communications Group |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CBETCMOnO3QC&dq=richard+tapia&pg=PT6 |access-date=7 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

Tapia received his [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] in mathematics in1961 from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]]. He then earned his [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] in mathematics, also from UCLA, in 1966. In 1968, he received his PhD from UCLA in mathematics with the dissertation "A Generalization of [[Newton's method|Newton's Method]] with an Application to the [[Euler–Lagrange equation|Euler–Lagrange Equation]]"<ref name="SIAM">{{cite web |access-date=November 15, 2008 |url=http://www.siam.org/news/news.php?id=495|title=Arlie Petters Is First Recipient of Blackwell-Tapia Prize|date=December 8, 2002 |first=Robert E. |last=Megginson|author-link= Robert Megginson |work=SIAM News|publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics}}</ref>, under advisors [[Magnus Hestenes]] and Charles Tompkins.<ref name="MathGenealogy">{{cite web|access-date=November 15, 2008|url=http://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=14920|title=Richard Tapia|work=Mathematics Genealogy Project }}</ref>
== Career ==
{{More citations needed section|date=June 2026}}His professional academic career began in 1968 when he accepted an assistant professor position at the Mathematics Research Center (MRC) at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. After two years there, he moved to Rice, where he remained.

=== University positions ===
* 1968–1970: Assistant Professor, [[Sterling Hall bombing#Army Mathematics Research Center|Army Mathematics Research Center]], [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]]
* 1970–1972: Assistant Professor of Mathematical Sciences, Rice University
* 1972–1976: Associate Professor of Mathematical Sciences, Rice University
* 1976–?: Professor of Mathematical Sciences, Rice University
* 1978–1983: Chair, Department of Mathematical Sciences, Rice University
* 1978–1983: Adjunct Professor, [[The Institute for Rehabilitation and Research|T.I.R.R.]], (then called the Texas Institute for Rehabilitation and Research) Baylor College of Medicine
* 1986–1988: Lecturer, Department of Community Medicine, [[Baylor College of Medicine]]
* 1989–2000: Director of Education and Outreach Programs, Center for Research on Parallel Computation, Rice University
* 1989–?: Associate Director of Graduate Studies, Office of Research and Graduate Studies, Rice University
* 1991–2005: Noah Harding Professor of Computational and Applied Mathematics, Rice University
* 1999–?: Director, Center for Excellence and Equity in Education, Rice University
* 2000–?: Adjunct Professor, College of Natural Sciences and Mathematics, University of Houston
* 2005–2026: Maxfield and Oshman Professor of Engineering, Rice University <ref name=RiceObit/>
* 2005–2026: University Professor, Rice University <ref name=RiceObit/>

===External positions===
* 1978–1991: Editor, ''[[SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis]]''
* 1981–1996: Editor, ''Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications''
* 1989–1992: Member, [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]] Board of Trustees
* 1990–1991: Editor, ''[[SIAM Journal on Optimization]]''
* 1992–1994: Member,  Mathematical Sciences Education Board, [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]] 
* 1992: Member, [[National Academy of Engineering]]
* 1996–2002: Member, [[National Science Board]]
* 2001-2004: Chair, Board on Higher Education and the Workforce, [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]]<ref name=Byrd />

===Publications===
Tapia published two books and authored or co-authored over 100 research papers in mathematics.<ref name=TapiaCenter-about>{{cite web |accessdate=July 3, 2025 |url=https://tapiacenter.rice.edu/people/professor-richard-tapia|title=Richard A. Tapia|work=About|publisher=Tapia Center, Rice University}}</ref>

In 2022 Tapia published ''Losing the Precious Few: How America Fails to Educate its Minorities in Science and Engineering''.<ref name=PreciousFew>{{Cite book |title=Losing the Precious Few: How America Fails to Educate its Minorities in Science and Engineering|first=Richard A |last=Tapia|url=https://artepublicopress.com/product/losing-the-precious-few-how-america-fails-to-educate-its-minorities-in-science-and-engineering/ |access-date=2024-10-11 |publisher=Arte Publico Press |language=en-US}}</ref> This book examines the lack of representation of domestic minority groups in [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] fields, identifying key causes such as standardized testing, gaps in K-12 education, and racial biases. He emphasizes the importance of improving access to higher education to address this disparity. The book offers insights for educators, students, and parents on fostering a more inclusive academic environment.<ref name=PreciousFew/>

== Personal life and death ==
Tapia married Jean Rodriguez Tapia. They were married 63 years at the time of her death in November 2022.<ref name=ACM-obit/> They had three children.<ref>{{cite book |title=Losing the Precious Few: How America Fails to Educate Its Minorities in Science and Engineering |first=Richard A. |last=Tapia |date=2022 |publisher=Arte Público Press |isbn=9781558859425 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4oK2zgEACAAJ |access-date=12 September 2023 |language=en|via=GoogleBooks.com}}</ref> Their daughter, Circee, was killed by a drunk driver in 1982.<ref name=50yrs-Chron>
{{cite news|accessdate=May 2, 2026 |url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/education/article/rice-tapia-50-years-honor-19381467.php
|work=[[Houston Chronicle]]
|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240425013811/https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/education/article/rice-tapia-50-years-honor-19381467.php |archive-date=April 25, 2024
|date=April 7, 2024 |title=Legendary Rice professor Richard Tapia honored for 50 years of research and mentorship|first=Samantha |last=Ketterer}}</ref>

Tapia died in 2026 in Houston at 88 from liver cancer.<ref name="nyt">{{cite web|title=Richard Tapia, Mathematician Who Pushed to Diversify His Field, Dies at 88|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/17/science/richard-a-tapia-dead.html|date=June 17, 2026|last=Williams|first=Alex|publisher=The New York Times|access-date=June 17, 2026}}</ref>{{efn|Published articles give his age as 88 at the time of death; though, other sources give his birthdate in March 1939<ref name=NSTMF>{{cite web|accessdate=March 9, 2025
|url=https://nationalmedals.org/laureate/richard-a-tapia/|title=Richard A. Tapia - 2010 National Medal of Science, Mathematics And Computer Science|publisher=National Science & Technology Medals Foundation}}</ref>}}<ref name=InformsDeath>{{cite web |accessdate=May 24, 2026 |url= https://connect.informs.org/discussion/the-passing-of-dr-richard-tapia-may-22-2026 |work=Informs
|title= The Passing of Dr. Richard Tapia -- May 22, 2026 | first=William
|last=Christian}}
</ref> 

== Awards and honors ==
[[File:Annual Awards Recognize Outstanding Contributions in Research and Public Service (14477038246).jpg|200px|thumb|right|Tapia accepting the [[Vannevar Bush Award]] in 2014.]]
In 1992 Tapia became the first Hispanic elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]].<ref name=Byrd />

In 1996 President [[Bill Clinton]] awarded Tapia the Presidential Award for Science, Mathematics, and Engineering Mentoring.<ref name=HouChron2024>{{cite news|accessdate=March 12, 2025|url=https://www.pressreader.com/usa/houston-chronicle/20240408/281513641179648?srsltid=AfmBOoo27YxS8i6q9hnKdUH6BAnVhgsqc7-s2hDZx7jQGtJ72zKSIUxB|work=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=April 8, 2024
|page=A1|first=Samantha |last=Ketterer
|title=Service defines longtime Rice prof - He's mentored and inspired students for more than 50 years}}</ref> That year, Clinton appointed Tapia to the [[National Science Board]], where he served until 2002.<ref name="Byrd">{{Cite web |last=Byrd |first=Sam |date=April 8, 2024 |title=Richard Tapia celebrated for 50 years of service at Rice |url=https://news.rice.edu/news/2024/richard-tapia-celebrated-50-years-service-rice |website=Rice News}}</ref>

In 2001 the first ''[[Association of Computing Machinery|ACM]] Richard Tapia Celebration of Diversity in Computing Conference'' was held in Houston with 164 attendees. The annual conference has grown to include thousands of attendees.<ref name=ACMTapiaConf-about>{{cite web|accessdate= July 3, 2025 |url=https://tapiaconference.cmd-it.org/about/about24-tapia-conference/ |title=About Tapia Conference: How it Began|publisher=Center for Minorities and People with Disabilities in IT (CMD-IT)}}</ref>

In 2004 Tapia received the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]] (SIAM) Prize for Distinguished Service to the Profession, in Portland, and [[AMS Distinguished Public Service Award|Distinguished Public Service Award]], [[American Mathematical Society]], in Phoenix.<ref>{{cite web |title=Societies: The SIAM Prize for Distinguished Service |url=http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Societies/SIAMService.html |work=The MacTutor History of Mathematics |publisher=University of St. Andrews}}</ref>

In 2009 he received [[Hispanic Heritage Foundation|Hispanic Heritage Award in Math and Science]].<ref>{{cite web |title=22nd Annual Hispanic Heritage Awards to Honor Latino Leaders During Star-Studded Ceremony on Capitol Hill |url=http://www.hispanicheritage.org/images/press/Press%20Release%202009%20HHA.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101219043002/http://hispanicheritage.org/images/press/Press%20Release%202009%20HHA.pdf |archive-date=19 December 2010 |access-date=11 January 2011 |publisher=Hispanic Heritage Awards}}</ref>

In 2010 he was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]] (Mathematics And Computer Science) "For his pioneering and fundamental contributions in optimization theory and numerical analysis and for his dedication and sustained efforts in fostering diversity and excellence in mathematics and science education."<ref name=2010-NMS>{{cite web|accessdate=2024-09-14
|url=https://nationalmedals.org/laureate/richard-a-tapia/
|title=Richard A Tapia|website=nationalmedals.org}}</ref> He received the award at the [[White House]] from President [[Barack Obama]] on October 21, 2011.<ref name=2010-Pres>{{cite web|accessdate=2024-09-14
|url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.jsp?recip_id=5300000000476
|title=The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details - Richard A Tapia
|publisher=[[National Science Foundation]]}}</ref>

In 2014 Tapia received the [[Vannevar Bush Award]] from the [[National Science Board]] for "his distinguished contributions to mathematics [and] extraordinary leadership in increasing opportunities for underrepresented minorities in science and mathematics", according to Ruth David, chair of the NSB's Committee on Honorary Awards.<ref name=VannevarBush2014>{{cite press release|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=130815|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812191902/https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=130815|archivedate=August 12, 2014|url-status=dead|title=Richard Tapia, mathematician and mentor, receives 2014 Vannevar Bush Award|date=	March 20, 2014|publisher=National Science Foundation}}</ref> Also in 2014, the [[Blackwell-Tapia prize]] and conference were named for Tapia and [[David Blackwell]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Buckmire |first1=R |date=2019 |title=Recognizing Black and Latinx Mathematical Excellence: The Blackwell–Tapia Prize |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201902/rnoti-p218.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |volume=66 |issue=2 |pages=218–220 |doi=10.1090/noti1798  |doi-access=free|access-date=20 October 2023}}</ref>
 
In 2016 Tapia received the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) Public Engagement with Science Award, recognizing him for his contributions to science, technology, engineering and mathematics education and public engagement.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|accessdate=June 11, 2025 |url=https://www.aaas.org/news/richard-tapia-wins-aaas-public-engagement-science-award
|title=Richard Tapia Wins the AAAS Public Engagement with Science Award|date=November 16, 2016 |first=Ginger |last=Pinholster
|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)}}</ref>

In 2021 he was named a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name=AMSfellow>{{citation |title=2021 Class of Fellows of the AMS |url=https://www.ams.org/cgi-bin/fellows/fellows_by_year.cgi?year=2021 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |access-date=2020-11-02}}</ref>

In 2026 the [[Harris County, Texas|Harris County]] [[Commissioners' court|commissioners]] unanimously voted to name the newly constructed Beltway 8 ship-channel bridge the ''Dr. Richard A. Tapia Bridge''. The commissioners noted that the structure was one of the most prominent pieces of infrastructure in the nation to be named after a Hispanic leader.<ref name=Bridge-Newsroom-2026/>

Tapia received honorary doctorates from [[Carnegie Mellon University]] and the [[Colorado School of Mines]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Newton |first1=David E. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oaMBpyYz5CEC&dq=richard+tapia&pg=PA226 |title=Latinos in Science, Math, and Professions |date=14 May 2014 |publisher=Infobase Publishing |isbn=978-1-4381-0786-8 |language=en}}</ref>
